classification.difficultyReason: Model repeated dilution as a changing concentration, then invert that concentration to obtain a required sample volume.

content.prompt: I take 900 mL of a liquid and dilute it with 100 mL of water. Then I take 900 mL of the mixture and again dilute it with 100 mL of water. I carry out 20 dilutions altogether.

children.label: a
children.prompt: What percentage of the final mixture is original liquid? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

answer.short:
$12.16\%$.

This is the concentration of original liquid after 20 dilutions altogether.
answer.worked:
Using 20 dilutions altogether, as indicated by the answer book: the first dilution gives concentration $\frac{900}{1000}=0.9$. Each subsequent dilution multiplies the concentration by $0.9$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Final concentration}&=0.9^{20}\\\text{Final percentage}&=0.9^{20}\times100\%\\\text{Final percentage}&\approx12.16\%\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: How much mixture should I take if I want it to contain 20 mL of the original liquid? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

answer.short:
$164.51\text{ mL}$.

Divide the required original-liquid volume by the unrounded concentration.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Required mixture volume}\times0.9^{20}&=20\text{ mL}\\\text{Required mixture volume}&=20\div0.9^{20}\text{ mL}\\\text{Required mixture volume}&\approx164.51\text{ mL}\end{align*}$$
